Every Runtime was handed the same "random" numbers. Upgrade if anything you run
mints ids, tokens or nonces in JavaScript.

`Math.random` was seeded from a constant, written when the engine was first
ported and never revisited, so every Runtime replayed one stream from its first
draw. A host that builds a Runtime per script got the same number every time,
and two hosts in different processes got the same numbers as each other. It
reached us as the textbook `uuidv4()` returning one UUID forever.

A pooled Runtime does advance the sequence, which is why this survived: it looks
right on a warm host and repeats on every cold one — a restart, a first message,
a run-once script.

- The process reads entropy once and each Runtime derives its own stream from
  it, decorrelated, so neither realms nor separate processes march in step.
- `GOANT_RANDOM_SEED` keeps the deterministic behaviour for a benchmark
  comparing two builds or a fuzzer replaying a failure. Opt-in, so nothing gets
  it by accident.

`crypto.getRandomValues` and `crypto.randomUUID` are the other half, and the
reason the first half was so easy to reach. There was no `crypto` at all, and
every id library in circulation feature-detects it and falls back to
`Math.random` when it is missing — so the weak generator was not the path nobody
took, it was the only one on offer. Both read the operating system's CSPRNG on
the call, with no per-Runtime state to seed or duplicate. There is no
`crypto.subtle`.

Binaries below are the `goant` CLI for six platforms. It runs the JIT by
default; `goant -jit=false` turns it off.

To embed the package: `go get github.com/robomotionio/goant` (the JIT is
opt-in there, via `WithJIT(true)`).
